examples.title: Length of one turn of a helix
examples.problem: Find the speed, and the length of one full turn ($0\le t\le 2\pi$), of the helix $\gamma(t)=(2\cos t,\ 2\sin t,\ 3t)$.
steps: Differentiate each component: $\gamma'(t)=(-2\sin t,\ 2\cos t,\ 3)$.
The speed is $|\gamma'(t)|=\sqrt{4\sin^2 t+4\cos^2 t+9}=\sqrt{13}$, a constant.
Integrate the speed over one turn: $L=\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{13}\,dt=2\pi\sqrt{13}\approx 22.65$.

Sanity check by unrolling the cylinder the helix lives on: one turn goes around a circle of length $2\pi\cdot 2=4\pi$ while climbing $3\cdot 2\pi=6\pi$. The hypotenuse is $\sqrt{(4\pi)^2+(6\pi)^2}=2\pi\sqrt{13}$.

examples.title: Tangent plane of a paraboloid
examples.problem: The surface $\mathbf r(u,v)=(u,\ v,\ u^2+v^2)$ passes through $P=(1,2,5)$ at $(u,v)=(1,2)$. Find $\mathbf r_u$, $\mathbf r_v$, a normal vector, and the equation of the tangent plane at $P$.
steps: Differentiate: $\mathbf r_u=(1,0,2u)$ and $\mathbf r_v=(0,1,2v)$. At $(1,2)$ these are $(1,0,2)$ and $(0,1,4)$.
Take the cross product: $\mathbf N=(1,0,2)\times(0,1,4)=(0\cdot4-2\cdot1,\ 2\cdot0-1\cdot4,\ 1\cdot1-0\cdot0)=(-2,-4,1)$.
The tangent plane is $\mathbf N\cdot(\mathbf x-P)=0$, that is $-2(x-1)-4(y-2)+(z-5)=0$, which simplifies to $z=2x+4y-5$.
Check that $\mathbf N$ is perpendicular to both tangent vectors: $(1,0,2)\cdot(-2,-4,1)=0$ and $(0,1,4)\cdot(-2,-4,1)=0$.

practice.prompt: A particle moves along $\gamma(t)=(t^2,\ 3t,\ t^3)$. Find its velocity vector $\gamma'(2)$.
hints: Differentiate each component separately.
$\gamma'(t)=(2t,\ 3,\ 3t^2)$. Now substitute $t=2$.

practice.prompt: Find the length of the curve $\gamma(t)=\big(t,\ t^2,\ \tfrac23 t^3\big)$ for $0\le t\le 3$.
hints: The length is $\int_0^3|\gamma'(t)|\,dt$. First find $\gamma'(t)$ and its squared length.
$|\gamma'|^2=1+4t^2+4t^4$. Notice that this is a perfect square.

practice.prompt: The surface $\mathbf r(u,v)=(u+v,\ u-v,\ uv)$ is regular at $(u,v)=(2,1)$. Find the normal vector $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$ there.
practice.solution: $\mathbf r_u=(1,1,v)=(1,1,1)$ and $\mathbf r_v=(1,-1,u)=(1,-1,2)$. Then $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=(1\cdot2-1\cdot(-1),\ 1\cdot1-1\cdot2,\ 1\cdot(-1)-1\cdot1)=(3,-1,-2)$.
hints: First compute $\mathbf r_u=(1,1,v)$ and $\mathbf r_v=(1,-1,u)$, then evaluate at $(2,1)$.
At $(2,1)$ you need $(1,1,1)\times(1,-1,2)$. Use $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=(a_2b_3-a_3b_2,\ a_3b_1-a_1b_3,\ a_1b_2-a_2b_1)$.

practice.prompt: The curves $\alpha(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$ for $0\le t\le 2\pi$ and $\beta(t)=(\cos 2t,\sin 2t)$ for $0\le t\le \pi$ both trace the unit circle exactly once. Which statement is true?
practice.solution: $|\alpha'|=1$ and $|\beta'|=2$. So $L_\alpha=1\cdot 2\pi=2\pi$ and $L_\beta=2\cdot\pi=2\pi$. Velocity depends on the parametrization; the traced path and its length do not.
hints: Compute $|\alpha'(t)|$ and $|\beta'(t)|$ separately.
Length is speed integrated over the parameter interval: multiply each speed by the length of its interval.
choices: They have the same length, $2\pi$, but $\beta$ moves with twice the speed of $\alpha$.
They have the same velocity vector at every point of the circle.
$\beta$ has length $\pi$, because its parameter interval is half as long.
$\beta$ moves with half the speed of $\alpha$, because it finishes in half the time.

practice.prompt: On the unit sphere $\mathbf r(\theta,\phi)=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \sin\theta\sin\phi,\ \cos\theta)$, a curve is given by $\theta(t)=t$, $\phi(t)=2t$. Find its speed at $t=\pi/3$.
practice.solution: $\theta'=1$ and $\phi'=2$. Since $\mathbf r_\theta\perp\mathbf r_\phi$, $|\gamma'|^2=\theta'^2|\mathbf r_\theta|^2+\phi'^2|\mathbf r_\phi|^2=1+4\sin^2\theta$. At $\theta=\pi/3$, $\sin^2\theta=\tfrac34$, so $|\gamma'|^2=1+3=4$ and the speed is $2$.
hints: The velocity is $\gamma'=\theta'\,\mathbf r_\theta+\phi'\,\mathbf r_\phi$.
On the unit sphere $|\mathbf r_\theta|=1$, $|\mathbf r_\phi|=\sin\theta$, and the two vectors are perpendicular, so you can add their squared lengths.

quiz.prompt: Consider the torus patch $\mathbf r(u,v)=\big((3+\cos v)\cos u,\ (3+\cos v)\sin u,\ \sin v\big)$. Find the length of the normal vector $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$ at $(u,v)=(\pi/2,\pi/3)$.
quiz.solution: $\mathbf r_u=(3+\cos v)(-\sin u,\cos u,0)$ has length $3+\cos v$. $\mathbf r_v=(-\sin v\cos u,\,-\sin v\sin u,\,\cos v)$ has length $1$, and $\mathbf r_u\cdot\mathbf r_v=0$. So $|\mathbf N|=3+\cos v$, which at $v=\pi/3$ equals $3+\tfrac12=\tfrac72$.
hints: Compute $\mathbf r_u$ and $\mathbf r_v$ and check whether they are perpendicular.
If $\mathbf r_u\perp\mathbf r_v$ then $|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v|=|\mathbf r_u|\,|\mathbf r_v|$. Find each length as a function of $v$.

quiz.prompt: Which of these parametrizations is regular (that is, has $\mathbf r_u$ and $\mathbf r_v$ linearly independent) at $(u,v)=(0,0)$?
quiz.solution: The paraboloid $(u,v,u^2+v^2)$: $\mathbf r_u=(1,0,0)$, $\mathbf r_v=(0,1,0)$, independent. The map $(u^2,v,uv)$: $\mathbf r_u=(2u,0,v)=\mathbf 0$ at the origin. The cone $(u\cos v,u\sin v,u)$: $\mathbf r_v=u(-\sin v,\cos v,0)=\mathbf 0$ at $u=0$. The sphere chart $(\cos u\cos v,\sin u\cos v,\sin v)$: $\mathbf r_u=(0,1,0)$ and $\mathbf r_v=(0,0,1)$, independent. The map $(u+v,u+v,u^2)$: $\mathbf r_u=(1,1,2u)=(1,1,0)$ and $\mathbf r_v=(1,1,0)$ are parallel.
hints: Compute both partial derivatives at $(0,0)$ and look for a zero vector or two parallel vectors.
choices: $\mathbf r(u,v)=(u,\ v,\ u^2+v^2)$
$\mathbf r(u,v)=(u^2,\ v,\ uv)$
$\mathbf r(u,v)=(u\cos v,\ u\sin v,\ u)$
$\mathbf r(u,v)=(\cos u\cos v,\ \sin u\cos v,\ \sin v)$
$\mathbf r(u,v)=(u+v,\ u+v,\ u^2)$

mistakes: Treating the parameter $t$ as distance travelled. It equals arc length only when the speed is $1$.
Computing length as $|\gamma(b)-\gamma(a)|$ (the straight-line distance) or as $\int\gamma'\,dt$ instead of integrating the speed $|\gamma'|$.
Trusting a parametrization at a point where $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\mathbf 0$, such as the poles of the sphere in $(\theta,\phi)$ coordinates.
lessons.title: Curves and surfaces
lessons.summary: Describe curves and surfaces with parametrizations, and compute velocity, speed, arc length, tangent vectors and normal vectors.
objectives: Compute the velocity, speed and arc length of a parametrized curve in space.
Describe a surface by a parametrization $\mathbf r(u,v)$ and find its coordinate curves and tangent vectors $\mathbf r_u$ and $\mathbf r_v$.
Find a normal vector and the tangent plane of a parametrized surface at a point.
lessons.reading: MIT 18.950 Differential Geometry: look up the opening material on parametrized curves and regular surfaces in 3-space (velocity, arc length, tangent plane, normal vector).
lessons.article:
A **curve** is the path of a moving point; a **surface** is a sheet that a point can slide over. To do calculus on them we describe both with formulas in parameters. This week you will see that those formulas are a choice: the same geometric object can be described in many ways.

### Curves as parametrized paths

A parametrized curve in space is a map $\gamma(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ for $t$ in an interval. Think of $t$ as time. The **velocity** is the derivative

$$\gamma'(t)=\big(x'(t),\,y'(t),\,z'(t)\big),$$

a vector tangent to the path at $\gamma(t)$. Its length $|\gamma'(t)|$ is the **speed**. The curve is **regular** if $\gamma'(t)\neq 0$ for all $t$, so the path has a tangent line everywhere.

Adding up the speed gives the **arc length**:

$$L=\int_a^b |\gamma'(t)|\,dt.$$

For the circle $\gamma(t)=(R\cos t,\,R\sin t)$ we get $\gamma'=(-R\sin t,\,R\cos t)$, speed $R$, and $L=2\pi R$ for $0\le t\le 2\pi$.

A path and a parametrization are different things. The maps $(\cos t,\sin t)$ and $(\cos 2t,\sin 2t)$ trace the same circle at different speeds. Velocity depends on the parametrization; the length of the traced path does not. When the speed is always $1$, the parameter itself measures distance along the curve: this is the **arc-length parametrization**.

### Surfaces as parametrized sheets

A parametrized surface is a map $\mathbf r(u,v)=(x,y,z)$ from a region of the $(u,v)$-plane into space. Hold $v$ fixed and vary $u$ to get a **coordinate curve**; do the same with $u$ fixed. Their velocities are

$$\mathbf r_u=\frac{\partial \mathbf r}{\partial u},\qquad \mathbf r_v=\frac{\partial \mathbf r}{\partial v}.$$

If $\mathbf r_u$ and $\mathbf r_v$ are linearly independent at a point, the surface is **regular** there. Their span is the **tangent plane**, and

$$\mathbf N=\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$$

is a **normal vector**, nonzero exactly when $\mathbf r_u,\mathbf r_v$ are independent.

Now draw any curve on the surface by choosing $u(t)$ and $v(t)$. By the chain rule its velocity is

$$\gamma'(t)=u'(t)\,\mathbf r_u+v'(t)\,\mathbf r_v.$$

So every tangent vector is a combination of $\mathbf r_u$ and $\mathbf r_v$, and the coefficients $u'$ and $v'$ are its **components**. **The components of a tangent vector depend on the coordinates you chose; the arrow itself does not.** That sentence is the seed of this whole course.

### Example: the sphere

For radius $a$, polar angle $\theta$ measured from the north pole and azimuth $\phi$:

$$\mathbf r(\theta,\phi)=a(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \sin\theta\sin\phi,\ \cos\theta).$$

Then $\mathbf r_\theta=a(\cos\theta\cos\phi,\cos\theta\sin\phi,-\sin\theta)$ has length $a$, and $\mathbf r_\phi=a\sin\theta(-\sin\phi,\cos\phi,0)$ has length $a\sin\theta$. The two are perpendicular, and

$$\mathbf N=a^2\sin\theta\,(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \sin\theta\sin\phi,\ \cos\theta)$$

points straight out of the sphere. At the poles $\sin\theta=0$, so $\mathbf r_\phi=\mathbf 0$ and $\mathbf N=\mathbf 0$: the parametrization breaks down there even though the sphere itself is perfectly smooth. The fault lies in the coordinates, not in the surface. That is the topic of next week.

examples.title: From polar components to Cartesian components
examples.problem: At the point with polar coordinates $(r,\theta)=(2,\pi/2)$, a tangent vector has polar components $(v^r,v^\theta)=(1,3)$. Find its Cartesian components $(v^x,v^y)$.
steps: Differentiate the transition map $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ to get the Jacobian $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$.
Evaluate it at $r=2$, $\theta=\pi/2$, where $\cos\theta=0$ and $\sin\theta=1$: $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
Multiply: $\begin{pmatrix}v^x\\ v^y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$.
Picture check: the point is $(0,2)$. One unit of $r$ goes straight up, giving $(0,1)$. Three units of $\theta$ go left by $3\cdot 2=6$, giving $(-6,0)$. The sum is $(-6,1)$.

practice.prompt: On the unit sphere, the chart $(\theta,\phi)$ with $\mathbf r=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \sin\theta\sin\phi,\ \cos\theta)$ has coordinate singularities at which points?
practice.solution: $\mathbf r_\phi=\sin\theta\,(-\sin\phi,\cos\phi,0)$ vanishes when $\sin\theta=0$, that is at both poles, where every $\phi$ gives the same point. The seam $\phi=0\equiv 2\pi$ is only a cut that can be moved by shifting the range of $\phi$; the map is perfectly regular there.
hints: A chart fails where the tangent vectors of the coordinate curves stop being independent.
Compute $|\mathbf r_\phi|=\sin\theta$ and ask where it vanishes.
choices: At the north and south poles, $\theta=0$ and $\theta=\pi$, where $\phi$ is undefined and $\mathbf r_\phi=\mathbf 0$.
Along the whole equator $\theta=\pi/2$, where $\mathbf r_\theta$ points straight down.
Only at the north pole; the south pole is fine because $\theta=\pi$ is an allowed value.
At every point with $\phi=0$, because $\phi=0$ and $\phi=2\pi$ name the same point.

practice.prompt: Parabolic coordinates $(\sigma,\tau)$ on the plane are defined by $x=\tfrac12(\sigma^2-\tau^2)$, $y=\sigma\tau$. Find the Jacobian determinant $\det\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(\sigma,\tau)}$ at $(\sigma,\tau)=(2,1)$.
practice.solution: $J=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma&-\tau\\ \tau&\sigma\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\ 1&2\end{pmatrix}$ at $(2,1)$, so $\det J=\sigma^2+\tau^2=4+1=5$.
hints: Write the $2\times2$ matrix with rows $(x_\sigma, x_\tau)$ and $(y_\sigma, y_\tau)$.
$x_\sigma=\sigma$, $x_\tau=-\tau$, $y_\sigma=\tau$, $y_\tau=\sigma$. Substitute $(2,1)$ and take the determinant.

practice.prompt: At the point $(x,y)=(3,4)$ a tangent vector has Cartesian components $(v^x,v^y)=(1,2)$. Find its polar components $(v^r,v^\theta)$, with $\theta$ measured in radians.
practice.solution: $v^r=\tfrac35\cdot1+\tfrac45\cdot2=\tfrac{11}{5}$ and $v^\theta=-\tfrac{4}{25}\cdot1+\tfrac{3}{25}\cdot2=\tfrac{2}{25}$. Check by converting back: $v^x=\cos\theta\,v^r-r\sin\theta\,v^\theta=\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac{11}{5}-4\cdot\tfrac{2}{25}=1$.
hints: Use the Jacobian $\partial(r,\theta)/\partial(x,y)$, built from $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and $\theta=\arctan(y/x)$, evaluated at $(3,4)$ where $r=5$.
$\partial r/\partial x=x/r$, $\partial r/\partial y=y/r$, $\partial\theta/\partial x=-y/r^2$, $\partial\theta/\partial y=x/r^2$.
At $(3,4)$ the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}3/5&4/5\\ -4/25&3/25\end{pmatrix}$. Multiply it by $(1,2)^T$.

practice.prompt: A curve is given in the polar chart by $r(t)=1+t$ and $\theta(t)=\tfrac{\pi}{2}t$. Find its velocity components $(\dot x,\dot y)$ in the Cartesian chart at $t=1$.
practice.solution: At $t=1$ the Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $(\dot r,\dot\theta)=(1,\pi/2)$. So $(\dot x,\dot y)=\big(-2\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{2},\ 1\big)=(-\pi,1)$.
hints: At $t=1$: $r=2$, $\theta=\pi/2$, $\dot r=1$ and $\dot\theta=\pi/2$. These are the velocity components in the polar chart.
Multiply the polar Jacobian $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$ by $(\dot r,\dot\theta)^T$.

practice.prompt: A spiral is given in the polar chart by $r(t)=t$, $\theta(t)=t$ for $t>0$. (a) Write its velocity components in the polar chart. (b) Write the curve in the Cartesian chart and differentiate to get its Cartesian velocity. (c) Show that (a) and (b) are related by the polar Jacobian. (d) At $t=2$, compare the Cartesian speed with the Euclidean size of the polar components $\sqrt{\dot r^2+\dot\theta^2}$, and explain the difference.
practice.solution: (a) $(\dot r,\dot\theta)=(1,1)$. (b) $x=t\cos t$, $y=t\sin t$, so $(\dot x,\dot y)=(\cos t-t\sin t,\ \sin t+t\cos t)$. (c) With $r=t$ the Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-t\sin t\\ \sin t&t\cos t\end{pmatrix}$, and multiplying it by $(1,1)^T$ gives exactly the vector in (b). (d) $\dot x^2+\dot y^2=1+t^2$, so the Cartesian speed at $t=2$ is $\sqrt5\approx 2.24$, while $\sqrt{\dot r^2+\dot\theta^2}=\sqrt2\approx1.41$. The polar components are not Euclidean components: $\dot\theta$ is an angular rate, and the true speed is $\sqrt{\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2}$. Turning components into lengths needs a metric, which comes in Week 5.
hints: In (c), build the Jacobian $\partial(x,y)/\partial(r,\theta)$ with $r=t$ and $\theta=t$, then multiply it by the vector from (a).
For (d), the Cartesian speed is $\sqrt{\dot x^2+\dot y^2}$. Simplify it using $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$.
rubric: States $(\dot r,\dot\theta)=(1,1)$ and the correct Cartesian velocity $(\cos t-t\sin t,\ \sin t+t\cos t)$.
Builds the Jacobian at $r=t$, $\theta=t$ and multiplies it by the polar components in the correct order to reproduce (b).
Finds the speeds $\sqrt5$ and $\sqrt2$ in (d) and explains that $\partial_\theta$ has length $r$, so the polar components are not Euclidean components.

quiz.prompt: On the unit sphere let $(\theta,\phi)$ be the usual spherical chart and $(X,Y)=\left(\dfrac{x}{1-z},\ \dfrac{y}{1-z}\right)$ the stereographic chart from the north pole. At the point with $(\theta,\phi)=(\pi/2,\,0)$ a tangent vector has components $(v^\theta,v^\phi)=(1,2)$. Find its components $(v^X,v^Y)$ in the stereographic chart.
quiz.solution: Using $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos\theta}=-\dfrac{1}{1-\cos\theta}$, at $(\pi/2,0)$ we get $\partial_\theta X=-1$, $\partial_\phi X=-\dfrac{\sin\theta\sin\phi}{1-\cos\theta}=0$, $\partial_\theta Y=0$ (it carries a factor $\sin\phi$) and $\partial_\phi Y=\dfrac{\sin\theta\cos\phi}{1-\cos\theta}=1$. So $J=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $(v^X,v^Y)=(-1,2)$.
hints: Write $X$ and $Y$ in terms of the angles: $X=\dfrac{\sin\theta\cos\phi}{1-\cos\theta}$ and $Y=\dfrac{\sin\theta\sin\phi}{1-\cos\theta}$.
The Jacobian has entries $\partial X/\partial\theta$, $\partial X/\partial\phi$, $\partial Y/\partial\theta$, $\partial Y/\partial\phi$ at $(\pi/2,0)$, where $\sin\phi=0$ and $\cos\phi=1$.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about the polar chart $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ on the plane are true?
quiz.solution: The determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$ is $r$; the second column has length $r$; level curves of $r$ and $\theta$ are circles and rays. The chart fails at the origin. And allowing all real $\theta$ gives each point infinitely many coordinate pairs, so $\theta$ must be restricted to an interval of length $2\pi$.
hints: Compute the two columns of the Jacobian and their lengths, and recall what happens at $r=0$.
choices: The Jacobian determinant $\det\partial(x,y)/\partial(r,\theta)$ equals $r$.
The chart is valid on the whole plane, including the origin.
Curves of constant $r$ are circles centred at the origin, and curves of constant $\theta$ are rays from the origin.
The tangent vector $\partial(x,y)/\partial\theta$ has Euclidean length $r$.
Because $\theta$ and $\theta+2\pi$ describe the same point, $\theta$ can range over all real numbers and each point still has exactly one coordinate pair.

mistakes: Using the Jacobian in the wrong direction, for example applying $\partial(x,y)/\partial(r,\theta)$ to Cartesian components instead of polar components.
Evaluating the Jacobian before choosing the point. Its entries depend on $r$ and $\theta$, so substitute the point first.
Treating $v^\theta$ as a speed. It is an angular rate, and the corresponding arrow has length $r\,|v^\theta|$ in the plane.
lessons.title: Coordinate charts
lessons.summary: Use charts on the plane and the sphere, convert between them with Jacobian matrices, and express one tangent vector in two charts.
objectives: Explain what a chart and a transition map are, and recognise where a chart fails.
Compute the Jacobian matrix of a change of coordinates.
Convert the components of a tangent vector from one chart to another.

lessons.article:
You already name the same point of the plane in two ways: Cartesian $(x,y)$ and polar $(r,\theta)$. Differential geometry makes this precise and asks the key question: what stays the same when you switch?

### Charts

A **chart** on a region $U$ of a surface (or of space) assigns to each point of $U$ a list of numbers, its **coordinates**, so that the assignment is smooth and invertible with a smooth inverse. On the plane, $(x,y)$ is a chart. The relations $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ make $(r,\theta)$ a chart too, but only away from the origin: at $r=0$ every value of $\theta$ gives the same point. This kind of failure is a **coordinate singularity**. The plane is fine; the chart is what breaks.

Maps of the Earth show why charts come in families. No single flat map covers the whole globe without a cut, so an atlas uses several overlapping maps. The sphere behaves the same way: the $(\theta,\phi)$ chart fails at the poles, and in fact no single chart can cover a whole sphere. Two suffice. Stereographic projection from the north pole $(0,0,1)$ uses

$$(X,Y)=\left(\frac{x}{1-z},\ \frac{y}{1-z}\right),$$

which works everywhere except the north pole itself. Projecting from the south pole covers the rest.

### Transition maps and Jacobians

Where two charts overlap, the **transition map** turns the coordinates $x^i$ of one chart into the coordinates $x'^a$ of the other. Its derivative is the **Jacobian matrix** $\partial x'^a/\partial x^i$, with row index $a$ and column index $i$. For polar to Cartesian,

$$\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det=r.$$

The determinant vanishes exactly at the singular point $r=0$. The Jacobian of the reverse transition is the matrix inverse.

### One vector, two sets of components

Write a curve in the old chart as $x^i(t)$. In the new chart its coordinates are $x'^a(x^1(t),\dots,x^n(t))$, and the chain rule gives the velocity components

$$\dot x'^{\,a}=\frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}\,\dot x^{\,i}.$$

(A repeated index is summed.) So **the Jacobian converts the components of a tangent vector from the old chart to the new chart.** The arrow has not changed; only the numbers describing it have.

Look at the columns of the polar Jacobian at $(r,\theta)=(2,\pi/2)$. The $r$-column is $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)=(0,1)$: one unit of $r$ moves you one unit up. The $\theta$-column is $(-r\sin\theta,\ r\cos\theta)=(-2,0)$: one unit of $\theta$ moves you two units to the left. Each column is the velocity of a coordinate curve. The polar coordinate directions are not unit vectors, and their lengths change from point to point.

examples.title: A vector acting on a function
examples.problem: In the plane let $f=x^2y$ and let $v=2\partial_x-\partial_y$ at the point $(1,3)$. Compute $v(f)$, and then find the same number as $df(v)$.
steps: Apply the operator: $v(f)=v^x\,\partial_xf+v^y\,\partial_yf$ with $v^x=2$ and $v^y=-1$.
The partial derivatives are $\partial_xf=2xy=6$ and $\partial_yf=x^2=1$ at $(1,3)$.

The differential at this point is $df=6\,dx+1\,dy$, a covector with components $(6,1)$. Pairing with $v$: $df(v)=6\cdot2+1\cdot(-1)=11$. The covector $df$ is the machine that turns a direction into a rate of change.

examples.title: A covector from Cartesian to polar components
examples.problem: At $(x,y)=(3,4)$ let $\omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy$. Find its polar components $(\omega_r,\omega_\theta)$ and check that pairing with the vector $v=(1,2)$ gives the same number in both charts.
steps: The Cartesian components at $(3,4)$ are $(\omega_x,\omega_y)=(-4,3)$.

Covectors use the factors $\partial x^i/\partial x'^a$, which are the entries of the polar Jacobian. At $r=5$, $\cos\theta=\tfrac35$, $\sin\theta=\tfrac45$ it is $J=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3/5&-4\\ 4/5&3\end{pmatrix}$, and $\omega'_a=J^i{}_a\,\omega_i$, that is $\omega'=J^T\omega$.
Compute $\omega_r=\tfrac35(-4)+\tfrac45(3)=0$ and $\omega_\theta=(-4)(-4)+3\cdot3=25$. So $\omega=25\,d\theta=r^2\,d\theta$ at this point.

The vector $v=(1,2)$ has polar components $(\tfrac{11}{5},\tfrac{2}{25})$. Then $\omega_rv^r+\omega_\theta v^\theta=0+25\cdot\tfrac{2}{25}=2$, and in Cartesian components $\omega_xv^x+\omega_yv^y=-4+6=2$. The pairing agrees.

practice.prompt: In $\mathbb{R}^3$ let $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ and let $v=\partial_x+2\partial_y-\partial_z$ be a tangent vector at the point $(1,2,3)$. Compute the directional derivative $v(f)$.
practice.solution: At $(1,2,3)$: $\partial_xf=6$, $\partial_yf=3$, $\partial_zf=2$. So $v(f)=1\cdot6+2\cdot3+(-1)\cdot2=10$.
hints: $v(f)=v^x\,\partial_xf+v^y\,\partial_yf+v^z\,\partial_zf$.
$\partial_xf=yz$, $\partial_yf=xz$, $\partial_zf=xy$. Evaluate each at $(1,2,3)$.

practice.prompt: The function $f=xy$ is written in the polar chart as $f=r^2\cos\theta\sin\theta$. Write $df=f_r\,dr+f_\theta\,d\theta$ and enter the component $f_\theta$.
practice.solution: $f_\theta=r^2\,\partial_\theta(\cos\theta\sin\theta)=r^2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)=r^2\cos2\theta$.
hints: The component of $d\theta$ in $df$ is the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $\theta$, holding $r$ fixed.
Differentiate $r^2\cos\theta\sin\theta$ with the product rule.

practice.prompt: A new chart is defined by $x'=x+2y$, $y'=y$. A covector has components $(\omega_x,\omega_y)=(3,1)$ in the old chart. Find its components $(\omega'_{x'},\omega'_{y'})$ in the new chart.
practice.solution: $\omega'_{x'}=1\cdot3+0\cdot1=3$ and $\omega'_{y'}=(-2)\cdot3+1\cdot1=-5$. Check with a vector: $v=(0,1)$ becomes $v'=(2,1)$, and $\omega(v)=1$ while $\omega'(v')=3\cdot2+(-5)\cdot1=1$.
hints: Solve for the old coordinates in terms of the new: $x=x'-2y'$, $y=y'$. Covector components use $\partial x^i/\partial x'^a$.
The needed derivatives are $\partial x/\partial x'=1$, $\partial x/\partial y'=-2$, $\partial y/\partial x'=0$, $\partial y/\partial y'=1$.
$\omega'_a=\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\omega_i$: for each $a$, add up $\omega_x\,\partial x/\partial x'^a+\omega_y\,\partial y/\partial x'^a$.

practice.prompt: At the point $(x,y)=(0,2)$, which has polar coordinates $(r,\theta)=(2,\pi/2)$, a covector has polar components $(\omega_r,\omega_\theta)=(3,4)$. Find its Cartesian components $(\omega_x,\omega_y)$.
practice.solution: At $(0,2)$: $\partial_xr=0$, $\partial_yr=1$, $\partial_x\theta=-\tfrac12$, $\partial_y\theta=0$. So $\omega_x=0\cdot3+(-\tfrac12)\cdot4=-2$ and $\omega_y=1\cdot3+0\cdot4=3$. Check: $\partial_\theta=(-2,0)$ in Cartesian, so $\omega(\partial_\theta)=(-2)(-2)=4=\omega_\theta$, and $\partial_r=(0,1)$ gives $\omega(\partial_r)=3=\omega_r$.
hints: Now go from polar to Cartesian, so the primed chart is the polar one, $x'^a=(r,\theta)$, and the unprimed chart is Cartesian, $x^i=(x,y)$. The Cartesian covector components are $\omega_i=\dfrac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}\,\omega'_a$, where $r,\theta$ are functions of $(x,y)$.
$\partial r/\partial x=x/r$, $\partial r/\partial y=y/r$, $\partial\theta/\partial x=-y/r^2$, $\partial\theta/\partial y=x/r^2$. Evaluate at $(0,2)$.

practice.prompt: Using the laws $v'^a=\dfrac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}v^i$ and $\omega'_a=\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\omega_i$, show that the number $\omega_iv^i$ is the same in every chart. Then explain in one or two sentences why the numbers $\partial f/\partial x^i$ are the components of a covector rather than of a vector.
practice.solution: $\omega'_av'^a=\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\omega_i\,\dfrac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^j}v^j=\left(\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\dfrac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^j}\right)\omega_iv^j=\delta^i_j\,\omega_iv^j=\omega_iv^i$, since summing the chain-rule product over $a$ gives $\partial x^i/\partial x^j=\delta^i_j$. For the second part, the chain rule gives $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x'^a}=\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}$, which is the covector law with the inverse Jacobian, not the vector law $v'^a=\dfrac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}v^i$. Equivalently, $df(v)=v(f)$ is a chart-independent number.
hints: Multiply the two transformed quantities and sum over the new index $a$.
The chain rule says $\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\dfrac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^j}=\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x^j}=\delta^i_j$.
rubric: Substitutes both transformation laws into $\omega'_av'^a$ and groups the two Jacobian factors that share the summed index $a$.
Uses the chain rule to replace the product of the two Jacobians by $\delta^i_j$ and concludes $\omega'_av'^a=\omega_iv^i$.
Shows that $\partial f/\partial x'^a=(\partial x^i/\partial x'^a)\,\partial f/\partial x^i$ and identifies this as the covector law.

quiz.prompt: Which of these lists of numbers transform like the components of a covector, $\omega'_a=\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\,\omega_i$?
quiz.solution: $\partial f/\partial x^i$ obey $\partial f/\partial x'^a=\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\partial f/\partial x^i$, the covector law. The numbers $\omega(\partial_i)$ do too, because $\partial'_a=\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\partial_i$ and $\omega$ is linear. The velocity components $dx^i/dt$ are vector components. The coordinates themselves are not components of any tangent vector: under a nonlinear change they transform by $x'^a(x)$, not by a Jacobian.
hints: Ask whether each list measures a rate along a direction (a vector) or assigns a number to each direction (a covector).
choices: The partial derivatives $\partial f/\partial x^i$ of a function $f$, the components of $df$.
The velocity components $dx^i/dt$ of a moving particle.
The numbers $\omega_i=\omega(\partial_i)$ obtained by feeding the coordinate basis vectors into one fixed linear map $\omega$ from tangent vectors to numbers.
The coordinates $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ of a point, listed as a column.

quiz.prompt: In the plane, the 1-form $\omega=y\,dx+x\,dy$ acts on a tangent vector $v$ at the point $(x,y)=(1,1)$ whose polar components there are $(v^r,v^\theta)=(2,1)$. Find $\omega(v)$.
quiz.solution: $f=\tfrac12r^2\sin2\theta$, so $df=r\sin2\theta\,dr+r^2\cos2\theta\,d\theta$. At $r=\sqrt2$, $\theta=\pi/4$: $\sin2\theta=1$ and $\cos2\theta=0$, so $df=\sqrt2\,dr$. Then $\omega(v)=\sqrt2\cdot2=2\sqrt2$. Cartesian check: $v^x=\sqrt2-1$, $v^y=\sqrt2+1$, and $\omega(v)=y\,v^x+x\,v^y=2\sqrt2$.
hints: $\omega=d(xy)$, so $\omega(v)$ is the rate of change of $f=xy$ along $v$. In polar form $f=r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta$.
At $(1,1)$, $r=\sqrt2$ and $\theta=\pi/4$. Differentiate $f$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta$ there, and combine with $(v^r,v^\theta)=(2,1)$.

mistakes: Transforming covector components with the vector Jacobian. Vectors use $\partial x'/\partial x$; covectors use $\partial x/\partial x'$.
Reading $dx^i$ as a "tiny displacement" and forgetting that it is a covector: $dx^i(\partial_j)=\delta^i_j$.
Assuming the gradient vector and $df$ have the same components in every chart. They agree in Cartesian coordinates only; elsewhere you need the metric (Week 5).
lessons.title: Tangent and cotangent spaces
lessons.summary: Treat tangent vectors as directional derivatives, build the space of covectors dual to them, and transform the components of each between charts.
objectives: Write a tangent vector as $v=v^i\partial_i$ and use it as a directional derivative of functions.
Compute the differential $df$ of a function and evaluate $df(v)$.
Transform vector and covector components between charts, and use the pairing $\omega_iv^i$ as a chart-independent check.
lessons.reading: MIT 18.950 Differential Geometry: look up tangent vectors, the differential of a function and 1-forms; for the derivative-operator viewpoint and the dual (cotangent) space use a supplement on smooth manifolds.
lessons.article:
A tangent vector says "move this way, this fast." The natural thing to do with such a direction is to differentiate: how fast does a function $f$ change if you move that way? This week's idea is to **define** a tangent vector by what it does to functions. That definition needs no surrounding space, and it works in every chart.

### Tangent vectors as derivatives

At a point $p$, a tangent vector $v$ gives a directional derivative $v(f)$. If a curve through $p$ has velocity $v$, the chain rule gives

$$v(f)=\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))\Big|_{t=0}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}\,\dot x^{\,i}.$$

Read this as an operator: $v=v^i\,\partial_i$, where $\partial_i=\partial/\partial x^i$ and $v^i=\dot x^i$ (repeated indices are summed). The $n$ operators $\partial_1,\dots,\partial_n$ form a basis of the **tangent space** $T_pM$, the set of all tangent vectors at $p$.

Change charts and the chain rule gives $\partial'_a=\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\,\partial_i$. The operator $v=v^i\partial_i=v'^a\partial'_a$ is the same in every chart, so its components obey the law from last week:

$$v'^a=\frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}\,v^i.$$

### Covectors

A **covector** $\omega$ at $p$ is a linear map that takes a tangent vector and returns a number. The covectors at $p$ form the **cotangent space** $T^*_pM$, also of dimension $n$. The main example is the **differential** of a function:

$$df(v)=v(f),\qquad df=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}\,dx^i.$$

The covectors $dx^i$ are the basis dual to $\partial_i$, meaning $dx^i(\partial_j)=\delta^i_j$ (equal to $1$ if $i=j$, else $0$). A general covector is $\omega=\omega_i\,dx^i$, and feeding it a vector gives

$$\omega(v)=\omega_i\,v^i.$$

### How components transform

Because $\omega'_a=\omega(\partial'_a)$, the formula for $\partial'_a$ gives

$$\omega'_a=\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\,\omega_i.$$

Compare with the vector law: the Jacobian factor is the **inverse** one, with old and new coordinates swapped. That is exactly what makes the pairing chart-independent:

$$\omega'_a v'^a=\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^j}\,\omega_i v^j=\delta^i_j\,\omega_i v^j=\omega_i v^i.$$

| | vector | covector |
|---|---|---|
| Index | upper, $v^i$ | lower, $\omega_i$ |
| Basis | $\partial_i$ | $dx^i$ |
| Law | $v'^a=\dfrac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}\,v^i$ | $\omega'_a=\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\,\omega_i$ |
| Typical example | velocity of a curve | differential $df$ of a function |

In Cartesian coordinates we often write the gradient as a column of numbers $\partial f/\partial x^i$ and treat it like a velocity. That is safe only because changes between Cartesian systems are rotations, where the matrix $A$ is orthogonal and $A^{-T}=A$, so the two laws coincide. In polar coordinates they differ, which is why we keep the two kinds of object apart.

examples.title: Transforming a (1,1) tensor
examples.problem: A tensor of type $(1,1)$ has matrix $T=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ (row index up, column index down) in coordinates $(x,y)$. The new chart is $x'=x+y$, $y'=y$. Find its matrix $T'$ in the new chart.
steps: The Jacobian is $A=\dfrac{\partial x'}{\partial x}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, and its inverse is $A^{-1}=\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial x'}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
One upper and one lower index give $T'^a{}_b=A^a{}_i\,T^i{}_j\,(A^{-1})^j{}_b$, that is $T'=A\,T\,A^{-1}$.
First $AT=\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$. Then $T'=\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$.
Check: the trace $5$ and the determinant $6$ are unchanged, as they are for any similarity transformation.

examples.title: The dot product in polar coordinates
examples.problem: In Cartesian coordinates the dot product is the $(0,2)$ tensor with components $g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$. Find its components $g'_{ab}$ in the polar chart.
steps: A $(0,2)$ tensor uses two factors $\partial x^i/\partial x'^a$. These are the entries of the polar Jacobian $J=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$, with row $i$ and column $a$.
The law $g'_{ab}=J^i{}_aJ^j{}_b\,\delta_{ij}$ is the matrix product $g'=J^TJ$.

Multiply: $J^TJ=\begin{pmatrix}\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta&0\\ 0&r^2\sin^2\theta+r^2\cos^2\theta\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&r^2\end{pmatrix}$, where the off-diagonal entries $-r\sin\theta\cos\theta+r\sin\theta\cos\theta$ cancel.

So $g'_{rr}=1$, $g'_{\theta\theta}=r^2$, $g'_{r\theta}=0$. A small displacement $(dr,d\theta)$ has squared length $dr^2+r^2\,d\theta^2$. This is the polar form of the dot product, and Week 5 builds on it.

practice.prompt: How many independent components does a symmetric tensor $S_{ij}$ of type $(0,2)$ have in four dimensions?
practice.solution: The independent entries are those with $i\le j$: $4+3+2+1=10$, which equals $\tfrac{4\cdot5}{2}$.
hints: Symmetry means $S_{ij}=S_{ji}$, so only the entries with $i\le j$ are independent.
Count the pairs $(i,j)$ with $1\le i\le j\le4$: there are $4+3+2+1$ of them.

practice.prompt: In one dimension change the chart by $x'=3x$. In the old chart a vector has component $v^x=6$, a covector has component $\omega_x=6$, and a $(0,2)$ tensor has component $g_{xx}=18$. Find the new components $(v'^{x'},\ \omega'_{x'},\ g'_{x'x'})$.
practice.solution: $v'=3\cdot6=18$, $\omega'=\tfrac13\cdot6=2$, $g'=\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac13\cdot18=2$. Check: the pairing $\omega v$ is $36$ in the old chart and $2\cdot18=36$ in the new one.
hints: Here $\partial x'/\partial x=3$. A vector index uses this factor; each lower index uses its inverse, $\partial x/\partial x'=\tfrac13$.
The vector picks up one factor of $3$, the covector one factor of $\tfrac13$, and the $(0,2)$ tensor two factors of $\tfrac13$.

practice.prompt: A tensor of type $(1,1)$ has matrix $T=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ (row index up, column index down) in coordinates $(x,y)$. The new chart is $x'=2x$, $y'=x+y$. Enter the new components in the order $(T'^1{}_1,\ T'^1{}_2,\ T'^2{}_1,\ T'^2{}_2)$.
practice.solution: $AT=\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\4&6\end{pmatrix}$, and $T'=AT\,A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2\cdot\frac12-4\cdot\frac12&4\\ 4\cdot\frac12-6\cdot\frac12&6\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&4\\-1&6\end{pmatrix}$. Check: the trace is $5$ before and after, and the determinant is $-2$ before and after.
hints: The Jacobian is $A=\partial x'/\partial x=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, and $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\-1/2&1\end{pmatrix}$.
One upper and one lower index: $T'=A\,T\,A^{-1}$. Multiply $AT$ first.

practice.prompt: Which formula gives the correct transformation law for a tensor $T^i{}_j$ of type $(1,1)$ when passing from coordinates $x$ to coordinates $x'$?
practice.solution: An upper index transforms like a vector, with $\partial x'^a/\partial x^i$. A lower index transforms like a covector, with $\partial x^j/\partial x'^b$. Only the formula with $\partial x'^a/\partial x^i$ and $\partial x^j/\partial x'^b$ does both. The others put the wrong Jacobian on one or both indices, and they also break the rule that a free index must sit in the same position on both sides of an equation.
hints: The upper index $a$ must appear upstairs on $x'^a$ in a numerator, and the lower index $b$ must appear downstairs in the denominator $\partial x'^b$.
Upper index: $\partial x'/\partial x$. Lower index: $\partial x/\partial x'$. Check which formula obeys both rules.
choices: $T'^a{}_b=\dfrac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}\,\dfrac{\partial x^j}{\partial x'^b}\,T^i{}_j$
$T'^a{}_b=\dfrac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}\,\dfrac{\partial x'^b}{\partial x^j}\,T^i{}_j$
$T'^a{}_b=\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\,\dfrac{\partial x'^b}{\partial x^j}\,T^i{}_j$
$T'^a{}_b=\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\,\dfrac{\partial x^j}{\partial x'^b}\,T^i{}_j$

practice.prompt: Prove that the trace $T^i{}_i$ of a $(1,1)$ tensor is a scalar, that is, $T'^a{}_a=T^i{}_i$ in every chart.
practice.solution: $T'^a{}_a=\dfrac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}\dfrac{\partial x^j}{\partial x'^a}\,T^i{}_j$. Summing over $a$, the chain rule gives $\dfrac{\partial x^j}{\partial x'^a}\dfrac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}=\dfrac{\partial x^j}{\partial x^i}=\delta^j_i$. Hence $T'^a{}_a=\delta^j_i\,T^i{}_j=T^i{}_i$. In matrix language, $\operatorname{tr}(ATA^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}T$.
hints: Set $b=a$ in the transformation law and sum over $a$.
The two Jacobian factors that share the index $a$ multiply to a Kronecker delta by the chain rule.
rubric: Writes the transformation law for $T'^a{}_b$ and sets $b=a$ with a sum over $a$.
Applies the chain rule to turn the product of the two Jacobian factors into $\delta^j_i$.
Concludes $T'^a{}_a=T^i{}_i$ and states that this makes the trace a scalar.

quiz.prompt: In parabolic coordinates, $x=\tfrac12(\sigma^2-\tau^2)$ and $y=\sigma\tau$, the dot product is a $(0,2)$ tensor with Cartesian components $\delta_{ij}$, so its new components are $g'_{ab}=\dfrac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\dfrac{\partial x^j}{\partial x'^b}\,\delta_{ij}$. Find $g'_{\sigma\sigma}$ at $(\sigma,\tau)=(3,1)$.
quiz.solution: $x_\sigma=\sigma$ and $y_\sigma=\tau$, so $g'_{\sigma\sigma}=\sigma^2+\tau^2=9+1=10$.
hints: With $a=b=\sigma$ the sum becomes $\sum_i\big(\partial x^i/\partial\sigma\big)^2$, the squared length of the vector $(x_\sigma,y_\sigma)$.
$x_\sigma=\sigma$ and $y_\sigma=\tau$.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following objects are tensors, meaning their components obey the tensor transformation law under every smooth change of coordinates?
quiz.solution: The trace is a contraction, so it is a scalar. The array $u^i\omega_j$ is a tensor product, of type $(1,1)$. Symmetrization only permutes indices and adds, which preserves the law. The array $\partial_jV^i$ picks up an extra term from the derivative of the Jacobian, and $v^i+\omega_i$ adds components that transform with opposite Jacobians, so it has no coordinate-independent meaning.
hints: Ask whether the object is built only from tensor products, contractions and index permutations of tensors, and whether the indices are used consistently.
choices: The trace $T^i{}_i$ of a $(1,1)$ tensor.
The array of partial derivatives $\partial_jV^i$ of a vector field $V$.
The array $u^i\omega_j$ built from a vector $u$ and a covector $\omega$.
The componentwise sum $v^i+\omega_i$ of a vector and a covector.
The symmetrized array $\tfrac12(S_{ij}+S_{ji})$ of a $(0,2)$ tensor $S$.

mistakes: Using $A$ where $A^{-1}$ belongs. Each upper index takes $\partial x'/\partial x$, and each lower index takes $\partial x/\partial x'$.
Applying the $(0,2)$ rule $A^{-T}TA^{-1}$ to a $(1,1)$ tensor, or the reverse. The index positions decide the rule.
Contracting two upper indices or two lower indices. Only an upper index paired with a lower index gives a tensor.
lessons.title: Tensors
lessons.summary: Define tensors as multilinear maps, transform their components between charts with one Jacobian factor per index, and use contraction and symmetry.
objectives: Read the type $(p,q)$ of a tensor from its indices and count its components.
Transform the components of a tensor between charts, using one Jacobian factor for each index.
Contract, symmetrize and antisymmetrize tensors, and distinguish true tensors from arrays that merely look like them.

lessons.article:
Scalars, vectors and covectors follow one pattern: a geometric quantity at a point, together with a rule saying how its components change with the chart. A **tensor** is the general version of that pattern.

### Tensors as multilinear maps

A tensor of **type $(p,q)$** at a point takes $p$ covectors and $q$ vectors and returns a number, and it is linear in each slot separately. Its **components** are its values on basis elements:

$$T^{i_1\dots i_p}{}_{j_1\dots j_q}=T\big(dx^{i_1},\dots,dx^{i_p},\ \partial_{j_1},\dots,\partial_{j_q}\big).$$

A scalar is $(0,0)$. A vector $v^i$ is $(1,0)$, since it eats a covector. A covector $\omega_i$ is $(0,1)$. A matrix $M^i{}_j$ acting as a linear map is $(1,1)$. A bilinear form such as the dot product, $g(u,v)=g_{ij}u^iv^j$, is $(0,2)$. In $n$ dimensions a $(p,q)$ tensor has $n^{p+q}$ components.

### The transformation law

Each upper index transforms like a vector index and each lower index like a covector index: one Jacobian factor per index.

$$T'^{a}{}_{b}=\frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}\,\frac{\partial x^j}{\partial x'^b}\,T^i{}_j,\qquad T'_{ab}=\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial x'^a}\,\frac{\partial x^j}{\partial x'^b}\,T_{ij}.$$

For a linear change $x'=Ax$ these are matrix products: $T'=A\,T\,A^{-1}$ for type $(1,1)$ and $T'=A^{-T}\,T\,A^{-1}$ for type $(0,2)$.

The law is linear and homogeneous, so a tensor that vanishes in one chart vanishes in every chart. That is why physical laws are written as tensor equations: a statement true in one coordinate system is true in all of them.

### Building new tensors

- **Tensor product:** multiply components, for example $(u\otimes\omega)^i{}_j=u^i\omega_j$, which has type $(1,1)$.
- **Contraction:** set an upper index equal to a lower index and sum. This lowers the type from $(p,q)$ to $(p-1,q-1)$. The pairing $\omega_iv^i$ and the trace $M^i{}_i$ are contractions. They are scalars: $\operatorname{tr}(AMA^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}M$.
- **Symmetry:** $S_{(ij)}=\tfrac12(S_{ij}+S_{ji})$ and $S_{[ij]}=\tfrac12(S_{ij}-S_{ji})$. A symmetric $(0,2)$ tensor has $n(n+1)/2$ independent components and an antisymmetric one has $n(n-1)/2$. Symmetry survives a change of chart.

### Not every array is a tensor

The coordinates $x^i$ are not the components of a vector. The partial derivatives $\partial_jV^i$ of a vector field are not a tensor either: when the Jacobian varies from point to point, differentiating $V'^a=\frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^i}V^i$ produces an extra term. Repairing this is the job of connections, in Weeks 7 and 8.

examples.title: The length of a circle of latitude
examples.problem: On a sphere of radius $a=2$, find the length of the circle of latitude $\theta=\pi/3$, traversed once with $\phi$ increasing from $0$ to $2\pi$.
steps: The metric is $ds^2=4\,(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)$, so $g_{\theta\theta}=4$ and $g_{\phi\phi}=4\sin^2\theta$.
Along the curve $\theta=\pi/3$ is constant, so $\dot\theta=0$, and take $\phi=t$, so $\dot\phi=1$.
The squared speed is $g_{\phi\phi}\dot\phi^2=4\sin^2(\pi/3)=3$, so the speed is $\sqrt3$.
Integrate: $L=\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt3\,dt=2\sqrt3\,\pi$.
Check: in space this is a circle of radius $a\sin\theta=2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=\sqrt3$, whose circumference is $2\pi\sqrt3$.

examples.title: A gradient vector in polar coordinates
examples.problem: Let $f=y=r\sin\theta$. Find the gradient vector $\nabla f$ in the polar chart, and check it against the Cartesian answer.
steps: The covector $df$ has polar components $(f_r,f_\theta)=(\sin\theta,\ r\cos\theta)$.
The inverse polar metric is $g^{ij}=\operatorname{diag}(1,\,1/r^2)$. Raising the index gives $(\nabla f)^r=\sin\theta$ and $(\nabla f)^\theta=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{r}$.
Convert to Cartesian components with the polar Jacobian: $(\nabla f)^x=\cos\theta\sin\theta-r\sin\theta\cdot\dfrac{\cos\theta}{r}=0$.
Similarly $(\nabla f)^y=\sin\theta\cdot\sin\theta+r\cos\theta\cdot\dfrac{\cos\theta}{r}=1$. The gradient of $y$ is $(0,1)$, as it must be.

practice.prompt: In polar coordinates the vector $v=3\,\partial_r+2\,\partial_\theta$ is attached to the point with $r=2$. Using the metric $ds^2=dr^2+r^2\,d\theta^2$, find its length $|v|$.
practice.solution: $|v|^2=1\cdot3^2+4\cdot2^2=9+16=25$, so $|v|=5$. The arrow has a radial part of length $3$ and a perpendicular angular part of length $r\cdot 2=4$: a 3-4-5 triangle.
hints: Because the metric is diagonal, $|v|^2=g_{rr}(v^r)^2+g_{\theta\theta}(v^\theta)^2$.
At $r=2$, $g_{rr}=1$ and $g_{\theta\theta}=r^2=4$.

practice.prompt: A curve in the plane is given in polar coordinates by $r(t)=e^t$, $\theta(t)=t$ for $0\le t\le\ln 2$. Find its length.
practice.solution: $\sqrt{\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2}=\sqrt{e^{2t}+e^{2t}}=\sqrt2\,e^t$. Then $L=\sqrt2\int_0^{\ln2}e^t\,dt=\sqrt2\,(2-1)=\sqrt2$.
hints: The length is $\int\sqrt{g_{ij}\dot x^i\dot x^j}\,dt=\int\sqrt{\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2}\,dt$.
Here $\dot r=e^t$, $r=e^t$ and $\dot\theta=1$, so the integrand is a constant multiple of $e^t$.

practice.prompt: In a chart $(x^1,x^2)$ a metric has components $g_{ij}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$. A covector has components $(\omega_1,\omega_2)=(5,5)$. Find the components $(\omega^1,\omega^2)$ of the corresponding vector, $\omega^i=g^{ij}\omega_j$.
practice.solution: $g^{ij}\omega_j=\tfrac15\,(3\cdot5-1\cdot5,\ -1\cdot5+2\cdot5)=\tfrac15\,(10,5)=(2,1)$. Check by lowering again: $g_{ij}\omega^j=(2\cdot2+1\cdot1,\ 1\cdot2+3\cdot1)=(5,5)$.
hints: The inverse of $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ is $\dfrac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$.
Here $\det g=5$ and $g^{ij}=\tfrac15\begin{pmatrix}3&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Multiply it by $(5,5)^T$.

practice.prompt: At the point of the plane with polar coordinate $r=2$, let $u=\partial_r$ and $v=\partial_r+\partial_\theta$. Using the metric $dr^2+r^2d\theta^2$, find $\cos\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the angle between $u$ and $v$.
practice.solution: $g(u,v)=g_{rr}\cdot1\cdot1=1$, $|u|=1$ and $|v|=\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt5$, so $\cos\alpha=1/\sqrt5\approx0.447$. In the plane: the radial unit vector and a vector with radial part $1$ and perpendicular part $2$ make an angle with $\tan\alpha=2$.
hints: $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{g(u,v)}{|u|\,|v|}$ with $g(u,v)=g_{ij}u^iv^j$.

practice.prompt: For the paraboloid $\mathbf r(u,v)=(u\cos v,\ u\sin v,\ u^2)$ the induced metric is $g_{ij}=\mathbf r_i\cdot\mathbf r_j$. Find $\det g$ as a function of $u$.
practice.solution: $g_{uu}=\cos^2v+\sin^2v+4u^2=1+4u^2$, $g_{vv}=u^2$ and $g_{uv}=-u\sin v\cos v+u\sin v\cos v=0$. So $\det g=u^2(1+4u^2)$, and the area element is $u\sqrt{1+4u^2}\,du\,dv$.
hints: First find $\mathbf r_u=(\cos v,\sin v,2u)$ and $\mathbf r_v=(-u\sin v,u\cos v,0)$.
Compute $g_{uu}=\mathbf r_u\cdot\mathbf r_u$, $g_{uv}=\mathbf r_u\cdot\mathbf r_v$ and $g_{vv}=\mathbf r_v\cdot\mathbf r_v$, then $\det g=g_{uu}g_{vv}-g_{uv}^2$.

quiz.prompt: Find the area of the zone of a sphere of radius $2$ between the latitudes $\theta=\pi/3$ and $\theta=2\pi/3$, using the area element $\sqrt{\det g}\,d\theta\,d\phi$.
quiz.solution: $A=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}4\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=2\pi\cdot4\,\big[-\cos\theta\big]_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}=8\pi\left(\tfrac12+\tfrac12\right)=8\pi$.
hints: For $ds^2=4\,(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)$, $\det g=16\sin^2\theta$, so $\sqrt{\det g}=4\sin\theta$ for $0<\theta<\pi$.
Integrate $4\sin\theta$ over $\theta\in[\pi/3,2\pi/3]$ and $\phi\in[0,2\pi]$.

quiz.prompt: Flat spacetime has the metric $ds^2=-dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$ (speed of light $1$), so $g(v,v)=-(v^t)^2+(v^x)^2+(v^y)^2+(v^z)^2$. Which of these vectors $(v^t,v^x,v^y,v^z)$ are timelike, that is, have $g(v,v)<0$?
hints: Compute $g(v,v)$ for each vector. Remember the minus sign on the time component.

mistakes: Treating $g_{\theta\theta}=r^2$ as a length. It is a squared length, so the vector $\partial_\theta$ has length $r$.
Inverting a non-diagonal metric entry by entry. The inverse metric is the matrix inverse; only for a diagonal metric is $g^{ii}=1/g_{ii}$.
Dropping the square root in $L=\int\sqrt{g_{ij}\dot x^i\dot x^j}\,dt$ or in the area element $\sqrt{\det g}$.
lessons.title: Metrics
lessons.summary: Measure lengths, angles and areas with a metric, raise and lower indices, and compute the induced metric of a surface.
objectives: Compute the length of a vector, the angle between two vectors and the length of a curve from the metric components $g_{ij}$.
Find the induced metric of a parametrized surface and its area element $\sqrt{\det g}$.
Raise and lower indices with $g^{ij}$ and $g_{ij}$, including for a Lorentzian signature.
lessons.reading: MIT 18.950 Differential Geometry: look up the first fundamental form of a surface (arc length, angles and area on a surface); for general Riemannian and Lorentzian metrics use a supplement.
lessons.article:
So far we can differentiate and transform, but we cannot measure. The polar vector $(v^r,v^\theta)=(1,1)$ has no length until we say how to measure it, and last week the dot product turned into $\operatorname{diag}(1,r^2)$ in polar coordinates. A **metric** is a rule for measuring, supplied at every point.

### The metric tensor

A **Riemannian metric** is a symmetric, positive-definite $(0,2)$ tensor field $g$. It gives the inner product, length and angle:

$$\langle u,v\rangle=g_{ij}u^iv^j,\qquad |v|=\sqrt{g_{ij}v^iv^j},\qquad \cos\alpha=\frac{g(u,v)}{|u|\,|v|}.$$

We usually package $g$ as the **line element** $ds^2=g_{ij}\,dx^i\,dx^j$. Three examples:

- The plane: $ds^2=dx^2+dy^2$ in Cartesian coordinates and $ds^2=dr^2+r^2\,d\theta^2$ in polar coordinates.
- The sphere of radius $a$: $ds^2=a^2\,(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)$.
- Any surface $\mathbf r(u,v)$ in space has the **induced metric** $g_{ij}=\mathbf r_i\cdot\mathbf r_j$, built from the tangent vectors of Week 1.

For the sphere, $\mathbf r_\theta\cdot\mathbf r_\theta=a^2$, $\mathbf r_\phi\cdot\mathbf r_\phi=a^2\sin^2\theta$ and $\mathbf r_\theta\cdot\mathbf r_\phi=0$, which gives the line element above.

### Lengths and areas

The length of a curve $x^i(t)$ is the integral of its speed:

$$L=\int_a^b\sqrt{g_{ij}\,\dot x^{\,i}\dot x^{\,j}}\;dt.$$

On a sphere of radius $a$, the latitude circle $\theta=\theta_0$ with $\phi=t$ has speed $a\sin\theta_0$, so $L=2\pi a\sin\theta_0$: shorter than the equator, as it should be. The area of a region is $\iint\sqrt{\det g}\;du\,dv$. For the sphere $\sqrt{\det g}=a^2\sin\theta$, and integrating over all angles gives the total area $4\pi a^2$.

### Raising and lowering indices

Because $g$ is invertible we can define the **inverse metric** $g^{ij}$ by $g^{ij}g_{jk}=\delta^i_k$. Then

$$v_i=g_{ij}\,v^j\quad(\text{lowering}),\qquad \omega^i=g^{ij}\,\omega_j\quad(\text{raising}).$$

The metric thus identifies vectors with covectors. This resolves the puzzle from Week 3: the **gradient vector** is $(\nabla f)^i=g^{ij}\partial_jf$, which in polar coordinates is $\partial_rf\,\partial_r+r^{-2}\,\partial_\theta f\,\partial_\theta$. It is not the same list of numbers as the covector $df$.

### Other signatures

In relativity the metric is **Lorentzian**, with signature $(-,+,+,+)$; for flat spacetime in units where the speed of light is $1$, $ds^2=-dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$. Now $g(v,v)$ can be negative (timelike), zero (null) or positive (spacelike). Raising and lowering use the same formulas, but a sign can flip: lowering the index of $v^\mu=(2,1,0,0)$ gives $v_\mu=(-2,1,0,0)$. This course uses mostly Riemannian metrics, but the algebra carries over unchanged.

examples.title: Integrating a 1-form around a circle
examples.problem: Let $\omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy$. Compute $\oint\omega$ around the unit circle traversed counterclockwise, and compare with the integral of $d\omega$ over the unit disk.
steps: Parametrize the circle by $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$, so $\dot x=-\sin t$ and $\dot y=\cos t$.
Substitute into the form: $\omega(\dot\gamma)=-y\,\dot x+x\,\dot y=\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$.
Integrate: $\oint\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi$.
Now $d\omega=\big(\partial_x(x)-\partial_y(-y)\big)\,dx\wedge dy=2\,dx\wedge dy$. The disk has area $\pi$, so $\int_Dd\omega=2\pi$, in agreement with $\int_S d\omega=\int_{\partial S}\omega$.

examples.title: The area form in polar coordinates
examples.problem: Express $dx\wedge dy$ in polar coordinates and use it to compute $\int dx\wedge dy$ over the half-annulus $1\le r\le2$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$.
steps: From $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$: $dx=\cos\theta\,dr-r\sin\theta\,d\theta$ and $dy=\sin\theta\,dr+r\cos\theta\,d\theta$.
Wedge them, using $dr\wedge dr=d\theta\wedge d\theta=0$ and $d\theta\wedge dr=-dr\wedge d\theta$: $dx\wedge dy=r\cos^2\theta\,dr\wedge d\theta-r\sin^2\theta\,d\theta\wedge dr=r\,dr\wedge d\theta$.
Integrate, taking $(r,\theta)$ as positively oriented: $\int_0^\pi\!\int_1^2r\,dr\,d\theta=\pi\cdot\tfrac32=\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$.
Check: the half-annulus has area $\tfrac12\pi\,(2^2-1^2)=\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

practice.prompt: Evaluate the 2-form $\beta=3\,dx\wedge dy$ on the pair of vectors $u=(2,1)$ and $v=(1,4)$, that is, find $\beta(u,v)$.
practice.solution: $(dx\wedge dy)(u,v)=2\cdot4-1\cdot1=7$, so $\beta(u,v)=3\cdot7=21$. This is $3$ times the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by $u$ and $v$.
hints: $(dx\wedge dy)(u,v)=u^xv^y-u^yv^x$.
Compute $2\cdot4-1\cdot1$ and multiply by $3$.

practice.prompt: Let $\omega=x^2y\,dx+xy\,dy$. Write $d\omega=h(x,y)\,dx\wedge dy$ and enter $h$.
practice.solution: $\partial_xQ=y$ and $\partial_yP=x^2$, so $h=y-x^2$.
hints: For $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ the coefficient is $\partial Q/\partial x-\partial P/\partial y$.
Here $P=x^2y$ and $Q=xy$.

practice.prompt: Compute $\int_\gamma\omega$ for $\omega=y\,dx+x^2\,dy$ along the parabola $\gamma(t)=(t,t^2)$, $0\le t\le1$.
practice.solution: $\omega(\dot\gamma)=y\dot x+x^2\dot y=t^2\cdot1+t^2\cdot2t=t^2+2t^3$. Then $\int_0^1(t^2+2t^3)\,dt=\tfrac13+\tfrac12=\tfrac56$.
hints: Substitute $x=t$, $y=t^2$, $dx=dt$ and $dy=2t\,dt$ into $\omega$.
The integrand becomes $t^2+t^2\cdot2t$.

practice.prompt: Which expression equals $dx\wedge dy$ in polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$?
practice.solution: The Jacobian determinant is $\cos\theta\cdot r\cos\theta-(-r\sin\theta)\sin\theta=r$, so $dx\wedge dy=r\,dr\wedge d\theta$. Dropping the factor $r$ forgets the Jacobian; $r\,d\theta\wedge dr=-r\,dr\wedge d\theta$ has the wrong orientation; and $r^2$ confuses the area form with the metric component $g_{\theta\theta}$.
hints: Compute $dx$ and $dy$ in terms of $dr$ and $d\theta$, then wedge them.
Equivalently, the coefficient of $dr\wedge d\theta$ is the Jacobian determinant $\det\partial(x,y)/\partial(r,\theta)$.
choices: $r\,dr\wedge d\theta$
$dr\wedge d\theta$
$r\,d\theta\wedge dr$
$r^2\,dr\wedge d\theta$

practice.prompt: On the unit sphere, with $ds^2=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2$, consider the latitude circle $\theta=\pi/3$ traversed once with $\phi$ increasing from $0$ to $2\pi$. Find (a) its length and (b) the integral $\oint\omega$ of the 1-form $\omega=(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi$ around it. Enter $(\text{a},\ \text{b})$.
practice.solution: (a) $L=\int_0^{2\pi}\sin(\pi/3)\,dt=\sqrt3\,\pi$. (b) $\oint\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}(1-\tfrac12)\,dt=\pi$. Notice that $d\omega=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$ is the area form of the sphere, so (b) is the area $2\pi(1-\cos\tfrac\pi3)=\pi$ of the polar cap $\theta\le\pi/3$. This number returns when we parallel transport vectors around the circle.
hints: Along the circle $\dot\theta=0$ and $\dot\phi=1$. The speed is $\sqrt{g_{\phi\phi}}=\sin\theta$, and the pullback of $\omega$ is $(1-\cos\theta)\,\dot\phi\,dt$.
Both integrands are constant on the circle, so each integral is $2\pi$ times a constant. Use $\sin(\pi/3)=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos(\pi/3)=\tfrac12$.

quiz.prompt: The map $x=u^2$, $y=uv$ sends the rectangle $0\le u\le1$, $0\le v\le2$ onto a region $S$ of the plane. Compute $\int_S y\,dx\wedge dy$, taking $(u,v)$ as positively oriented.
quiz.solution: $dx\wedge dy=\det\begin{pmatrix}2u&0\\v&u\end{pmatrix}du\wedge dv=2u^2\,du\wedge dv$. So $\int_Sy\,dx\wedge dy=\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^2(uv)(2u^2)\,dv\,du=2\int_0^1u^3\,du\int_0^2v\,dv=2\cdot\tfrac14\cdot2=1$.
hints: Pull back: $dx=2u\,du$ and $dy=v\,du+u\,dv$. Then $dx\wedge dy=2u\cdot u\,du\wedge dv$.
The pulled-back integrand is $y\cdot2u^2=2u^3v$. Integrate over $0\le u\le1$ and $0\le v\le2$.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about differential forms are true?
quiz.solution: $d^2=0$ holds because mixed partials commute. The wedge is antisymmetric, so $dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx$. Reversing the direction of travel flips the sign of a line integral, while reparametrizing in the same direction leaves it unchanged. The correct coefficient in $d\omega$ is $\partial_xQ-\partial_yP$; for $\omega=x\,dy$ it gives $d\omega=dx\wedge dy$, not $-dx\wedge dy$.
hints: Recall that the wedge product is antisymmetric, and check the formula for $d\omega$ on a simple example such as $\omega=x\,dy$.
choices: $d(d\omega)=0$ for every form $\omega$.
$dx\wedge dy=dy\wedge dx$.
Traversing a curve in the opposite direction changes the sign of $\int_\gamma\omega$ for a $1$-form $\omega$.
For $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$, $d\omega=(\partial_xP-\partial_yQ)\,dx\wedge dy$.
Reparametrizing a curve in the same direction does not change $\int_\gamma\omega$.

mistakes: Forgetting that $dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy$. Swapping the order of a wedge flips the sign of the integral.
Replacing $dx\wedge dy$ by $dr\wedge d\theta$ and dropping the Jacobian factor $r$.
Writing $d(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=(\partial_xP-\partial_yQ)\,dx\wedge dy$. The correct coefficient is $\partial_xQ-\partial_yP$.
lessons.title: Differential forms
lessons.summary: Compute wedge products and exterior derivatives, and integrate 1-forms along curves and 2-forms over regions by pulling them back.
objectives: Evaluate wedge products and compute $d\omega$ for simple 1-forms, checking that $d^2=0$.
Pull back a form along a curve or a parametrized region to turn it into an ordinary integral.
Explain why the Jacobian determinant appears when a 2-form is written in new coordinates.
lessons.reading: MIT 18.950 Differential Geometry: look up differential forms, the exterior derivative, and integration of forms on curves and surfaces; use a supplement for the general $k$-form wedge product.
lessons.article:
Last week's metric lets us measure. Integration needs something different, and simpler: an object that eats a small oriented piece of a curve or surface and returns a number. For curves that object is a covector, which eats one tangent vector. For surfaces it must eat **two** tangent vectors (the sides of a small parallelogram) and return a signed area. Such objects are **differential forms**, and they need no metric at all.

### Forms and the wedge product

A **$k$-form** is an antisymmetric $(0,k)$ tensor field. A $0$-form is a function and a $1$-form is $\omega=\omega_i\,dx^i$. The **wedge product** of two $1$-forms is the $2$-form

$$(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)=\alpha(u)\,\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\,\beta(u).$$

So $dx\wedge dy$ sends $u,v$ to $u^xv^y-u^yv^x$, the signed area of the parallelogram they span. Swapping the arguments flips the sign: $dx^i\wedge dx^j=-dx^j\wedge dx^i$, and in particular $dx\wedge dx=0$. In $n$ dimensions a $k$-form has $\binom{n}{k}$ independent components.

### The exterior derivative

The operator $d$ turns a $k$-form into a $(k+1)$-form. On functions $df=\partial_if\,dx^i$. For a $1$-form $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ in the plane,

$$d\omega=\Big(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\Big)\,dx\wedge dy.$$

Two facts matter. First, $d(d\alpha)=0$ always: mixed partial derivatives commute, while the wedge is antisymmetric. Second, $d$ uses only partial derivatives yet produces a tensor, because the antisymmetrization cancels the extra term that spoils $\partial_jV^i$. In $\mathbb{R}^3$, $d$ on $0$-, $1$- and $2$-forms is the gradient, curl and divergence, and $d^2=0$ says $\nabla\times\nabla f=0$ and $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf F)=0$.

### Pullback and integration

To integrate a $1$-form along a curve $\gamma(t)$, substitute the curve into the form and integrate over the parameter:

$$\int_\gamma\omega=\int_a^b\omega_i(\gamma(t))\,\dot x^{\,i}(t)\,dt.$$

Reversing the direction of travel flips the sign; reparametrizing in the same direction changes nothing. For a surface piece $(u,v)\mapsto(x,y)$, substituting $dx$ and $dy$ gives

$$dx\wedge dy=\det\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\;du\wedge dv,$$

so the Jacobian determinant appears automatically. In polar coordinates $dx\wedge dy=r\,dr\wedge d\theta$.

One theorem ties integration to $d$: for a region $S$ with boundary $\partial S$ (oriented consistently),

$$\int_S d\omega=\int_{\partial S}\omega.$$

In the plane it says that the circulation of $\omega$ around a loop equals the integral of $d\omega$ over the enclosed region.

examples.title: Christoffel symbols of the polar metric
examples.problem: Use $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\tfrac12 g^{kl}(\partial_ig_{jl}+\partial_jg_{il}-\partial_lg_{ij})$ to find all Christoffel symbols for $ds^2=dr^2+r^2\,d\theta^2$.
steps: The metric is $g_{rr}=1$, $g_{\theta\theta}=r^2$, with inverse $g^{rr}=1$, $g^{\theta\theta}=r^{-2}$. The only nonzero derivative of a component is $\partial_rg_{\theta\theta}=2r$.

Because $g^{kl}$ is diagonal, $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\tfrac12 g^{kk}(\partial_ig_{jk}+\partial_jg_{ik}-\partial_kg_{ij})$. For $k=r$ and $i=j=\theta$ only the last term survives: $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=\tfrac12\cdot1\cdot(-\partial_rg_{\theta\theta})=-r$.

For $k=\theta$ and $(i,j)=(r,\theta)$ only the first term survives: $\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}=\tfrac12\cdot r^{-2}\cdot\partial_rg_{\theta\theta}=\tfrac{2r}{2r^2}=\tfrac1r$. By symmetry $\Gamma^\theta_{\theta r}=\tfrac1r$ too.

Every other combination contains only derivatives that vanish, such as $\partial_\theta g_{\theta\theta}$ or $\partial_rg_{rr}$. So the nonzero symbols are $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=-r$ and $\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}=\Gamma^\theta_{\theta r}=1/r$.

examples.title: A diagonal metric with an exponential factor
examples.problem: Find the nonzero Christoffel symbols of $ds^2=dx^2+e^{2x}\,dy^2$.
steps: Here $g_{xx}=1$ and $g_{yy}=e^{2x}$. The only nonzero derivative of a component is $\partial_xg_{yy}=2e^{2x}$.
Apply the diagonal recipe with $i=x$, $j=y$: $\Gamma^x_{yy}=-\dfrac{\partial_xg_{yy}}{2g_{xx}}=-e^{2x}$.
With $i=y$, $j=x$: $\Gamma^y_{yx}=\Gamma^y_{xy}=\dfrac{\partial_xg_{yy}}{2g_{yy}}=\dfrac{2e^{2x}}{2e^{2x}}=1$.
The remaining candidates need $\partial_yg_{xx}$, $\partial_yg_{yy}$ or $\partial_xg_{xx}$, which are all zero. So only $\Gamma^x_{yy}=-e^{2x}$ and $\Gamma^y_{xy}=\Gamma^y_{yx}=1$ are nonzero.

practice.prompt: In polar coordinates, the vector field $V=\partial_r$ has constant components $(V^r,V^\theta)=(1,0)$. Which statement is correct?
practice.solution: $\partial_r$ is the outward radial unit vector. It points along $+x$ at $(1,0)$ and along $+y$ at $(0,1)$, so it is not constant even though $\partial_jV^i=0$. The covariant derivative detects this: $\nabla_\theta V^\theta=\partial_\theta V^\theta+\Gamma^\theta_{\theta r}V^r=\tfrac1r\neq0$. Whether a field is covariantly constant is chart-independent; only the partial derivatives of components are not.
hints: Picture the field in the plane. Which way does $\partial_r$ point at the point $(1,0)$, and which way at $(0,1)$?
choices: Its components do not change, yet the field is not constant: it points in a different direction at each point. The connection term $\Gamma^i_{jk}V^k$ accounts for this.
The field is constant, because the partial derivatives $\partial_jV^i$ of its components all vanish.
The field is not constant, because all the Christoffel symbols vanish in polar coordinates.
Whether a field is constant depends on the chart, so no chart-independent statement is possible.

practice.prompt: Consider the metric $ds^2=dx^2+x^4\,dy^2$ in coordinates $(x,y)$. Find the Christoffel symbols $(\Gamma^y_{xy},\ \Gamma^x_{yy})$ at $x=3$.
practice.solution: $\Gamma^y_{xy}=\dfrac{4x^3}{2x^4}=\dfrac2x=\dfrac23$ and $\Gamma^x_{yy}=-\dfrac{4x^3}{2\cdot1}=-2x^3=-54$.
hints: The metric is diagonal with $g_{xx}=1$ and $g_{yy}=x^4$. Use $\Gamma^y_{xy}=\dfrac{\partial_xg_{yy}}{2g_{yy}}$ and $\Gamma^x_{yy}=-\dfrac{\partial_xg_{yy}}{2g_{xx}}$.
$\partial_xg_{yy}=4x^3$.

practice.prompt: For the unit sphere, $ds^2=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2$, enter the Christoffel symbol $\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}$ as a function of $\theta$.
practice.solution: $\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}=-\dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2\cdot1}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$.
hints: Only $g_{\phi\phi}=\sin^2\theta$ varies, and only with $\theta$. Use $\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}=-\dfrac{\partial_\theta g_{\phi\phi}}{2g_{\theta\theta}}$.
$\partial_\theta(\sin^2\theta)=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $g_{\theta\theta}=1$.

practice.prompt: Consider the metric $ds^2=dx^2+2x\,dx\,dy+(1+x^2)\,dy^2$, that is $g_{xx}=1$, $g_{xy}=x$, $g_{yy}=1+x^2$. Find $(\Gamma^x_{xx},\ \Gamma^x_{yy},\ \Gamma^y_{xy})$ at $x=1$.
practice.solution: Lowered: $\Gamma_{y,xx}=\partial_xg_{xy}=1$, $\Gamma_{x,xx}=0$, $\Gamma_{x,yy}=\partial_yg_{xy}-\tfrac12\partial_xg_{yy}=-x$, $\Gamma_{y,xy}=\tfrac12\partial_xg_{yy}=x$, $\Gamma_{x,xy}=0$. Raise: $\Gamma^x_{xx}=g^{xx}\Gamma_{x,xx}+g^{xy}\Gamma_{y,xx}=-x$, $\Gamma^x_{yy}=g^{xx}\Gamma_{x,yy}=(1+x^2)(-x)$ and $\Gamma^y_{xy}=g^{yx}\Gamma_{x,xy}+g^{yy}\Gamma_{y,xy}=x$. At $x=1$: $(-1,-2,1)$.
hints: This metric is not diagonal, so use the full formula. Here $\det g=1$ and $g^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1+x^2&-x\\-x&1\end{pmatrix}$.

First compute the lowered symbols $\Gamma_{l,ij}=\tfrac12(\partial_ig_{jl}+\partial_jg_{il}-\partial_lg_{ij})$, then raise with $g^{kl}$. Only $x$-derivatives are nonzero: $\partial_xg_{xy}=1$ and $\partial_xg_{yy}=2x$.

practice.prompt: Let $ds^2=dr^2+G(r)^2\,d\theta^2$ for a positive function $G$. Show that the only nonzero Christoffel symbols are $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=-GG'$ and $\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}=\Gamma^\theta_{\theta r}=G'/G$. Then read off the polar case and the case of the unit sphere (where $r$ plays the role of the polar angle $\theta$ and $\theta$ plays the role of $\phi$).
practice.solution: With $g_{rr}=1$ and $g_{\theta\theta}=G^2$, the only nonzero derivative is $\partial_rg_{\theta\theta}=2GG'$. Then $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=-\dfrac{\partial_rg_{\theta\theta}}{2g_{rr}}=-GG'$ and $\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}=\Gamma^\theta_{\theta r}=\dfrac{\partial_rg_{\theta\theta}}{2g_{\theta\theta}}=\dfrac{2GG'}{2G^2}=\dfrac{G'}{G}$. The symbols $\Gamma^r_{rr}$, $\Gamma^r_{r\theta}$, $\Gamma^\theta_{rr}$ and $\Gamma^\theta_{\theta\theta}$ each need a derivative with respect to $\theta$ or of $g_{rr}$, so they vanish. For polar coordinates $G=r$ gives $(-r,\,1/r)$. For the unit sphere $G=\sin r$ gives $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=-\sin r\cos r$ and $\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}=\cot r$.
hints: The only nonzero derivative of a metric component is $\partial_rg_{\theta\theta}=2GG'$.
Use the diagonal recipe, and check each of the remaining four independent symbols to see that it vanishes.
rubric: Identifies $\partial_rg_{\theta\theta}=2GG'$ as the only nonzero derivative of a metric component.
Computes $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=-GG'$ and $\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}=G'/G$ from the formula, and explains why the other symbols vanish.
Substitutes $G=r$ and $G=\sin r$ to recover the polar and sphere symbols.

quiz.prompt: The upper half-plane metric is $ds^2=\dfrac{dx^2+dy^2}{y^2}$ for $y>0$. Find $(\Gamma^x_{xy},\ \Gamma^y_{xx},\ \Gamma^y_{yy})$ at $y=2$.
quiz.solution: $\dfrac{\partial_yg_{xx}}{2g_{xx}}=\dfrac{-2y^{-3}}{2y^{-2}}=-\dfrac1y$, so $\Gamma^x_{xy}=-\dfrac1y$ and $\Gamma^y_{yy}=-\dfrac1y$. Also $\Gamma^y_{xx}=-\dfrac{-2y^{-3}}{2y^{-2}}=\dfrac1y$. At $y=2$: $(-\tfrac12,\ \tfrac12,\ -\tfrac12)$.
hints: Here $g_{xx}=g_{yy}=y^{-2}$, which depends only on $y$, and $\partial_yg_{xx}=\partial_yg_{yy}=-2y^{-3}$.
Use the diagonal recipe: $\Gamma^x_{xy}=\dfrac{\partial_yg_{xx}}{2g_{xx}}$, $\Gamma^y_{xx}=-\dfrac{\partial_yg_{xx}}{2g_{yy}}$ and $\Gamma^y_{yy}=\dfrac{\partial_yg_{yy}}{2g_{yy}}$.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about the Christoffel symbols of a metric are true?
quiz.solution: Polar coordinates on the plane show the symbols are not tensorial and need not vanish for a flat metric. Under $g\to cg$ the inverse scales as $c^{-1}$ and each derivative as $c$, so $\Gamma$ is unchanged. The formula contains only first derivatives of $g$. Torsion-freeness is the symmetry $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\Gamma^k_{ji}$.
hints: Look at the formula: how many derivatives of $g$ appear, and what happens to $g^{kl}$ and $\partial g$ when $g\to c\,g$?
choices: They are not tensor components: for the flat plane they vanish in Cartesian coordinates but not in polar coordinates.
Multiplying the metric by a positive constant, $g\to c\,g$, leaves them unchanged.
For a flat metric they vanish in every coordinate chart.
They involve second derivatives of the metric components.
They are symmetric in the two lower indices, $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\Gamma^k_{ji}$.

mistakes: Treating $\Gamma^k_{ij}$ as tensor components. They vanish in Cartesian coordinates on the plane but not in polar coordinates, so they cannot be a tensor.
Multiplying by $g_{kk}$ instead of dividing: the raised index needs the inverse metric, so a diagonal metric gives $\tfrac{1}{2g_{kk}}$.
Dropping a term of the combination $\partial_ig_{jl}+\partial_jg_{il}-\partial_lg_{ij}$, or flipping the sign of the last one.
